title: Narada sings the names
hookLine: a harmonium, a drum, one voice, and a whole room singing it back
tomorrow: who are the singers with a drum on the city sidewalk?
last: NO RULES OF TIME, PLACE OR PURITY.

lines: A HARMONIUM WHEEZES INTO A CHORD.
cards: A student hall on a Friday night, chairs pushed to the walls. Someone pumps a harmonium and it wheezes into a chord. A drum picks up the beat.

One voice sings a short line of names, and the room sings it back, a little ragged. Then again, a little faster. At the back, a first-timer who swears she can't sing is reading the words off a friend's lips.
A few rounds in, her mouth is moving. Soon, nobody in the room is the audience. How did that happen?

teach.h: NARADA: A SERVANT BOY WHO HEARD THE SAGES SING.
teach.b: That's kirtan: singing God's names and glories, often in call and response. And the Bhagavata Purana has a singer at its heart. Narada tells the sage Vyasa his own story.

In an earlier life he was a servant woman's little boy, sweeping and fetching for wandering sages who stayed through one rainy season. Every day he heard them sing about the Lord, and the singing got into him.
When his mother died, the boy walked off alone, sat under a tree and, for one moment, saw God in his heart. Then the vision was gone, and a voice told him the longing it left would carry him home.

teach.h: HE SINGS, AND THE LORD APPEARS IN HIS HEART.
teach.b: Now Narada wanders the worlds with his vina, and he says that when he sings the Lord's names, the Lord appears in his heart, as if called.
A servant boy who could perform no grand ritual, made a sage by hearing and singing.

teach.h: SANKIRTANA: THE WORSHIP OF THE WISE.
teach.b: That's why the same Purana says that in the age of Kali the wise worship through sankirtana, singing the names together. Not a sacrifice only priests can perform.

teach.h: A SONG THE ONE AT THE BACK CAN JOIN.
teach.b: A song the one at the back can join.
A pop chorus with a chant in it is not a kirtan. But it carried the sound of one home, and soon someone would take the singing out onto the street.

how: Kirtan is sung in temples, homes and halls with harmonium, drums and small cymbals: a leader sings a line of God's names and the group answers.

games.q: what does “the beatles and the mantra” mean?
o: a Sanskrit song the band was taught to perform on stage
a quiet word and a sung chant, both carried home from India
a concert tour the band played across India's temples

games.q: who's in the room — tap the pairs.
p: a servant boy who heard the sages sing
carried while he sings across the worlds

s: kirtan is a concert, with singers up front and an audience
it's call and response: the room answers, so nobody stays the audience.
in the Bhagavata Purana, singing God's names together is for priests only
it calls sankirtana the worship of the wise in the age of Kali, a song anyone can join.
in the Bhagavata, Narada began as a servant boy who heard sages singing
he learned by hearing and singing, and now carries the names across the worlds.

games.q: at a family puja, your uncle leads a bhajan and your teenage cousins stand at the back with their phones, 'just watching.' what would make it kirtan?
o: everyone answering the line, even softly, so no one is just watching.
a better speaker, so the leader's voice reaches the back of the room.
a trained singer up front, so the music sounds the way it should.
games.why: kirtan is call and response: one voice sings the names, and the room sings them back. the Bhagavata calls singing them together the worship of the wise.

practice: Try a little kirtan on your own. Pick a short line of names Hindus sing, like Hare Krishna, Hare Rama, or Om Namah Shivaya; if you don't pray, one word you hold dear.
Sing or hum it softly, then pause, as if a room were singing it back, and let the pause be as full as the line. Keep that rhythm, call and quiet answer, until the breath settles into it.

wordCard.voice: The Beatles and the mantra: from a silent word in Rishikesh to names sung together in kirtan, the last stop on this road.

orig.note: Sanskrit kirtana, singing God's names and glories; sankirtana is singing them together.

carryVoice: For the road, from Narada's song: sankirtana, God's names sung together, where the room answers the voice. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.5.32 (in the Kali age the wise worship through sankirtana)

Bhagavata Purana 1.5–1.6 (Narada tells Vyasa of his life as a maidservant's son who served the sages and heard their songs; now he wanders with his vina, and the Lord appears in his heart when he sings)
